tldr: Various sampling-based MPC methods such as MPPI and CEM are unified under a single Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) framework, organized along three axes: proposal, update rule, and resampling threshold. From this perspective, incorporating resampling and designing flexible proposals dramatically boost performance on long-horizon and contact-rich tasks.
hero_caption: Trajectory generation via SMC in a 5×5 obstacle field. At each step, particles are extended by one knot and weighted by cumulative cost. When the effective sample size drops, adaptive resampling is triggered, transitioning smoothly from multi-modal exploration in the early stages to focusing on the optimal path in the late stages.
overview:
Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) is a powerful approach that solves nonlinear, non-convex control problems purely through forward simulation without computing gradients. However, as the planning horizon grows longer, simple Gaussian perturbations suffer from severe drawbacks: multi-modality collapses into a single mode, and importance weights degenerate, drastically hurting exploration efficiency.

To address this, the authors reframe MPC as posterior inference in a generative model whose likelihood is the negative exponential of cost. This formulation matches Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), also known as particle filtering. This paper shows that prominent sampling-based MPC algorithms—such as Predictive Sampling, MPPI, and CEM—can all be unified under a single SMC algorithm specified by choices along three independent axes: proposal, update rule, and resampling threshold.

The authors evaluate this framework on MuJoCo control benchmarks in simulation, obstacle-field navigation, 7-DoF arm motion planning, and a non-prehensile push-T task on a physical Franka FR3 robot. The results show that resampling—pruning and duplicating particles mid-horizon—prevents weight degeneracy at long horizons, reducing collision rates by 30% in navigation. Furthermore, using a programmable proposal that incorporates task structure boosts success on the hardware push-T task from around 10% with standard Gaussian baselines up to 90%.
contributions: Formulated a unified SMC-based framework that characterizes sampling-based MPC algorithms such as Predictive Sampling, MPPI, and CEM along three independent axes: proposal, update rule, and resampling threshold.
Enabled mid-horizon resampling and flexible, arbitrary proposal distributions by propagating weighted particle sets rather than parametric distribution parameters across iterations.
Demonstrated the effectiveness of resampling and the critical importance of programmable proposals across long-horizon navigation, 7-DoF motion planning, and real-robot push-T tasks.
Overcame the particle count limitations of conventional SMC planners by releasing an open-source JAX implementation that runs in parallel on GPUs in real time.

sections.heading: Limitations of Sampling-based MPC and Unification via SMC
sections.summary: While sampling-based MPC is gradient-free and versatile, it suffers from weight degeneracy and mode collapse over long horizons. The authors formulate trajectory optimization as Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference, unifying major existing methods into a single framework to address these issues.
sections.details:
Model predictive control (MPC) has achieved great success in autonomous driving, humanoid robotics, and dynamic manipulation. In particular, sampling-based MPC offers a strong advantage: one can tune the compute-versus-quality tradeoff simply by varying the number of forward simulation rollouts. It also applies directly to nonlinear dynamics and non-convex costs where gradients are hard to define.

However, as the planning horizon (number of lookahead steps) grows longer, it encounters two major problems:
- Exploration via Gaussian perturbations collapses multi-modal search spaces with multiple viable paths down to a single mode.
- Importance weights become heavily skewed—a phenomenon known as weight degeneracy—which severely degrades exploration capability.

Many sampling-based methods (such as MPPI and CEM) update control inputs across all steps at once. While this leverages time-wise parallelism, it ignores the sequential structure of trajectories. In this work, the authors treat the negative exponential of the cost as a likelihood and reframe MPC as posterior inference. Using Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC, an extension of particle filters), they build a unified framework that alternates proposing candidate trajectories (particles), weighting by likelihood, and resampling.

The core contribution of this paper is decomposing and organizing diverse sampling-based MPC methods along three orthogonal axes: proposal, update rule, and resampling threshold. Coupled with a fast GPU-accelerated JAX implementation, the authors demonstrate its effectiveness across a variety of tasks, including real-robot experiments.

sections.heading: Probabilistic Inference for Control and Lineage of Sampling-based MPC
sections.summary: In the context of control as probabilistic inference in graphical models, this work applies SMC directly to online planning. Unlike prior unification efforts that propagate distribution parameters, this approach propagates particle sets, enabling resampling.
sections.details:
Viewing optimal control as probabilistic inference on a graphical model is a well-established idea. Trajectory optimization can be framed as approximate posterior inference. SMC is a natural fit for handling this sequential structure. Prior works have applied SMC to reinforcement learning, planning, and autonomous driving. However, they often relied on pre-trained policies or value functions, or their particles collapsed to Dirac distributions at local extrema. In contrast, the authors' approach runs at inference time using only programmed dynamics and costs, maintaining a full approximation of the control distribution.

Prominent sampling-based MPC methods include MPPI (based on path integral control), Biased-MPPI (mixing in an auxiliary controller), CEM (the cross-entropy method updating Gaussian parameters from elite samples), and iCEM (using temporally correlated noise). While originally proposed as separate algorithms, the authors' framework clarifies that they differ only in their proposals and update rules.

Recent work has also sought to unify MPC algorithms using variational inference, online learning, or Bregman divergences. However, most previous unifications update and propagate distribution parameters (such as mean and covariance) across iterations, projecting back into a parametric family. In contrast, this paper propagates the weighted particle set and its ancestral history directly. This allows resampling—pruning and duplicating particles at intermediate horizon steps—to be introduced as an independent design axis.

sections.heading: Formulating MPC as Probabilistic Inference
sections.summary: The MPC optimization problem is reformulated as posterior inference under a likelihood defined by exponentiated negative cost. Classical MPC corresponds to Maximum A-Posteriori (MAP) estimation, whereas sampling-based MPC estimates the expectation over the control distribution.
sections.details:
Under deterministic state transitions $x_{t+1} = D_\theta(x_t, u_t)$, standard MPC aims to minimize a total cost over a finite horizon $H$: $S(x_0, \mathbf{u}; \theta) = C_{\mathrm{term}}(x_H; \theta) + \sum_{t=0}^{H-1} C_t(x_t, u_t; \theta)$.

### III-A Model Predictive Control as Approximate Inference
To turn this into probabilistic inference, an auxiliary binary optimality variable $\mathcal{O} \in \{0, 1\}$ is introduced. The likelihood of being optimal is defined as the negative exponential of total cost: $p(\mathcal{O}=1 \mid x_0, \mathbf{u}; \theta) = \exp(-S(x_0, \mathbf{u}; \theta))$.

Letting $q(\mathbf{u} \mid x_0; \theta)$ be the uncontrolled input prior (proposal), Bayes' rule yields the target controlled posterior:
$p(\mathbf{u} \mid \mathcal{O}=1, x_0; \theta) \propto q(\mathbf{u} \mid x_0; \theta) \exp(-S(x_0, \mathbf{u}; \theta))$

When the prior is uniform, finding the minimum-cost sequence in classical MPC matches Maximum A-Posteriori (MAP) estimation on this posterior. Meanwhile, sampling-based MPC methods like MPPI compute the expected value (mean) of the input sequence under this posterior to decide the action. However, the normalizing constant (partition function) in the denominator is a high-dimensional path integral over the entire space and cannot be computed analytically. This motivates using SMC to evaluate particles sequentially decomposed across time.

sections.heading: A Unified Decomposition of Sampling-based MPC via SMC
sections.summary: A trajectory generation framework is built using Sequential Importance Sampling with Resampling (SIS/R). Sampling-based MPC is cleanly characterized as combinations along three independent axes: proposal, resampling threshold, and update rule.
sections.details:
Because the exponentiated total cost factors into a product over time steps, intermediate target distributions can be defined. In standard SIS/R (Sequential Importance Sampling with Resampling), each particle (trajectory) is extended by one step, its weight is updated, and resampling is performed whenever the effective sample size (ESS)—measuring weight dispersion—falls below a threshold $\rho \in [0, 1]$.

### IV-A A Unifying Decomposition
Within this framework, sampling-based MPC is fully described by three independent axes:
- **Proposal $q$**: The sampler generating candidate control inputs. Beyond Gaussian perturbations around a nominal plan, one can freely design mixture distributions that incorporate task-specific heuristics.
- **Resampling threshold $\rho$**: The ESS ratio criterion for triggering resampling. $\rho=0$ corresponds to Sequential Importance Sampling (SIS) without resampling, while $\rho > 0$ yields SIS/R with resampling.
- **Update rule $U$**: The rule used to reduce $K$ weighted samples down to the nominal plan $\mu$ that is ultimately executed.

When resampling is enabled, ancestor indices are tracked at each step. Backtracking from the final horizon step reconstructs the complete trajectory in $O(HK)$ time.

### IV-A 1 Recovering MPC Baselines
Combining these three axes cleanly recovers standard baselines:
- **Predictive Sampling (PS)**: Gaussian perturbation proposal, $\rho=0$ (no resampling), and the MAP update rule $U_{\mathrm{MAP}}$ choosing the sample with maximum weight.
- **MPPI**: Gaussian perturbation proposal, $\rho=0$, and the cost-weighted mean update rule $U_{\mathrm{mean}}$. Swapping the proposal for an auxiliary controller yields **Biased-MPPI**.
- **CEM**: Gaussian perturbation proposal, $\rho=0$, and the elite-sample mean and variance update rule $U_{\mathrm{elite}}$. Using temporally correlated noise yields **iCEM**.

This shows that the distinction between MPPI and CEM is essentially just a difference in update rules. Conventional methods have all been confined to the special case of $\rho=0$ (no resampling within the horizon).

sections.heading: Empirical Impact of Resampling and Proposals
sections.summary: Experiments across obstacle navigation, 7-DoF arm planning, and push-T tasks in simulation and hardware demonstrate that resampling drastically cuts collisions over long horizons, while programmable proposals dramatically boost success on contact-rich tasks.
sections.details:
To evaluate the impact of the three axes, extensive experiments were conducted in simulation and on a Franka FR3 robot.

### V-A 2D Kinematic Bicycle
This domain evaluates a kinematic bicycle model navigating an obstacle field toward a goal on a 2D plane. The horizon was varied from 5 to 28 knots, comparing performance with and without resampling ($\rho=0$ vs $\rho > 0$).
- At short horizons (5 knots), the difference is small. At a long horizon of 28 knots, the difference is striking.
- Under the MAP update, the collision rate dropped by about 30%, from 0.95 without resampling (SIS) to 0.66 with resampling (SIS/R). The median distance to the goal also improved dramatically from 8.6 to 2.2.
- Without resampling, particles that enter unavoidable collision regions early on survive throughout the horizon, wasting sampling budget.

### V-B 7-DoF Motion Planning
The benchmark uses MotionBenchMaker across 7 environments (100 problems each) for 7-DoF Franka FR3 collision-free motion planning.
- Introducing a programmable proposal—combining goal pose, local Gaussian perturbations, and uniform sampling within joint limits—boosted success rates to 78–86%, compared to 13–36% for standard Gaussian proposals.
- Adding resampling yielded an additional 4–7 percentage point improvement in success rate.

### V-C Closed-Loop Manipulation: Push-T in Simulation
A circular end-effector pushes a T-shaped block to a target around obstacles in a contact-rich task. A 3-component proposal program was designed: moving toward the T-block, orbiting around it, and local random walk.
- **Obstacle scaling**: As obstacle count increased, Gaussian proposal baselines (PS, MPPI, CEM, DIAL-MPC) collapsed, reaching nearly 0% success with 7 obstacles. In contrast, programmable proposals (Biased-PS, Biased-MPPI, Biased-CEM) maintained 92–100% success.
- **Particle efficiency**: With the proposal program, using just 16 particles (Biased-PS: 96%) outperformed the standard Gaussian proposal using 2048 particles (PS: 81%). High-quality solutions were found with over two orders of magnitude fewer particles.

### V-D Closed-Loop Manipulation: Push-T on Hardware
A real-world Push-T experiment was conducted on a Franka FR3 with poses tracked by OptiTrack (20 trials).
- Baselines with Gaussian proposals (PS, MPPI, DIAL-MPC) achieved only 10% success, and CEM achieved 15%.
- In contrast, Biased-PS and Biased-MPPI with the proposal program achieved 90% and 75% success rates, respectively.

sections.heading: Discussion and Outlook: Which Axes Really Matter?
sections.summary: Ablation experiments reveal that the proposal and resampling—not the update rule—are the decisive factors in sampling-based MPC. The study also highlights subtle dynamics, such as side effects of resampling in ultra-low particle regimes.
sections.details:
The most insightful takeaway from the experiments is that the long-debated choice of update rule—weighted average in MPPI versus elite selection in CEM—is not the dominant factor as task difficulty increases. What truly dictates success is designing **proposals** that generate high-quality candidates and using **resampling** to prune unpromising particles over long horizons.

### Observed Limitations and Open Challenges
- **Pitfalls of resampling with tiny particle budgets**: In Push-T, when the particle count was dropped to an extreme low of 16, adding resampling actually lowered the success rate from 96% to 64%. In complex contact spaces, early resampling risks prematurely collapsing particle diversity. Combining resampling with temperature scheduling (annealing) is needed.
- **Reliance on accurate models**: Real-robot experiments relied on high-precision motion capture, known CAD models, and fast replanning. While MPC feedback compensates for discrepancies between simulated contacts and real friction, extending the framework to explicitly handle state estimation uncertainty remains an important direction.

takeaways: Diverse sampling-based MPC methods like MPPI and CEM differ primarily in their update rules and can be unified as special cases of SMC without resampling.
Performance degradation in long-horizon planning is driven by weight degeneracy; adaptive mid-horizon resampling significantly reduces collision rates.
In challenging contact-rich and obstacle-cluttered tasks, tuning update rules matters far less than designing proposal distributions that incorporate domain knowledge or heuristics.
With an effective proposal, high success rates can be achieved using two orders of magnitude fewer particles (1/100 the compute) compared to Gaussian perturbation baselines.
limitations: In contact-rich settings with extremely small particle counts, resampling can prematurely collapse particle diversity and harm performance.
The tested proposal programs remain relatively simple; integrating learned policies or diffusion models as proposals remains open for exploration.
Real-robot validation assumed accurate OptiTrack pose tracking and precise CAD models, without explicitly planning under state uncertainty.
